summary: The article explains how the cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon), domesticated only about 200 years ago, became a Thanksgiving staple. It covers cranberry history and cultivation, unusual botanical traits like hermaphroditic flowers and air pockets, and what genomics reveals about breeding and evolution. It ends with why cranberries fit the Thanksgiving harvest window and how the industry has expanded.
one_line: Cranberries, domesticated only ~200 years ago, have a distinctive biology and genetics and became a Thanksgiving staple through harvest timing and tartness.
key_facts: Cultivated cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) was domesticated around 200 years ago, versus about 5,500 years for sorghum, 8,700 for corn and 5,000 for cotton.
Native Americans used wild cranberries in puddings, sauces, breads and pemmican, a portable high-protein food of dried meat and rendered animal fat sometimes studded with dried fruits.
Cranberry cultivation began in 1816 in Massachusetts, when Revolutionary War veteran Henry Hall found that covering bogs with sand fertilized the vines and retained water around roots.
Wisconsin produces roughly 60% of the U.S. cranberry harvest, followed by Massachusetts, Oregon and New Jersey; Canada also grows cranberries as a major fruit crop.
Cranberry flowers are hermaphroditic, so they can self-pollinate; otherwise they rely on bumblebees and honeybees.
The flower's resemblance to a bird's beak earned the cranberry its original name, the 'craneberry'.
Cranberries can be propagated sexually by seeds (more genetic diversity) or asexually by rooting vine cuttings (clones of high-performing varieties).
Every cranberry contains four air pockets, which make them float during bog flooding for harvest and bounce when fresh; the pockets let berries disperse seeds via water.
The cranberry is a diploid with 24 chromosomes, and its genome is less than one-tenth the size of the human genome.
Researchers compare the cultivated cranberry with its wild relative, the 'small cranberry' (Vaccinium oxycoccos), to locate valuable traits and the source of cold hardiness.
Molecular markers are being developed to help breeders combine genes for traits such as larger, firmer or redder fruit.
Fresh cranberries are harvested from mid-September through mid-November, so Thanksgiving falls within that window.
Cranberry sauce was loosely described in 1600s colonial accounts and first appeared in a cookbook in 1796.
Cranberries are more than twice as acidic as most other edible fruits, and the industry now sells juices and snacks to reach year-round markets.
